title: HCPCS Level II Purpose

sections.learningObjectives:
- Explain the purpose of HCPCS Level II and identify the types of items and services it reports.
- Describe the alphanumeric structure of HCPCS Level II codes and the categories identified by the leading letter.
- Relate HCPCS Level II to CPT (Level I) and determine when each code set is used.
- Apply accuracy, verification, and scope-of-practice principles when handling HCPCS Level II codes in the medical office.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

HCPCS is the full name for the big list of medical codes that everyone uses to name the same service or supply the same way, like giving every item in a store the same barcode.

### Question 2

Think of HCPCS as a two-shelf bookcase: the top shelf is CPT for doctor procedures, and the bottom shelf is Level II for supplies, medicines, and equipment.

### Question 3

Level I is the CPT book, the list of numbers used for the things doctors and clinicians actually do for a patient.

### Question 4

CMS is like the librarian who keeps the Level II shelf of codes organized and up to date for the whole country.

### Question 5

CPT covers what a doctor does; Level II covers all the extra stuff patients also need, like bandages, wheelchairs, medicines, and rides in an ambulance.

### Question 6

A bed for home is a piece of equipment, so it gets a Level II code. A visit or surgery is something the doctor does, so it gets a CPT code.

### Question 7

Every Level II code looks like one letter followed by four numbers, like a license plate: a letter that tells you the kind of item, then four numbers.

### Question 8

E0143 is the right shape: one letter and four numbers. The other choices look like different kinds of codes.

### Question 9

The first letter is like the aisle sign in a store: it tells you which section the item belongs in before you read the rest of the code.

### Question 10

J codes are the labels for medicines that are given by a shot or through an IV, not pills swallowed at home.

### Question 11

E stands for equipment, like a wheelchair or a hospital bed that a patient uses at home.

### Question 12

L codes are for braces and artificial body parts, like a knee brace or a replacement limb.

### Question 13

A codes are for the little supplies (like bandages and trays) and for rides in an ambulance.

### Question 14

DME is equipment a patient keeps and uses again and again at home, like a wheelchair or a hospital bed, not something thrown away after one use.

### Question 15

An oxygen machine stays in the patient's home and is used every day, so it is equipment; gloves and drapes are used once and thrown away.

### Question 16

CPT is for what the doctor does, and Level II is for the extra items, like a wheelchair or a shot, so the office uses both lists together.

### Question 17

If the doctor's work already has a CPT code, use it. Level II is only for the things CPT does not have a code for.

### Question 18

A modifier is a tiny add-on tag that gives extra detail, like writing which foot a shoe brace is for.

### Question 19

Level II modifiers can use letters, like RT for the right side, so the payer knows exactly which side an item is for.

### Question 20

Level III used to be different codes for different regions, but that got confusing, so it was mostly retired in favor of one national Level II list.

### Question 21

Picking the right code is a job for someone who is trained in coding; the assistant helps by typing things in correctly and double-checking them.

### Question 22

A doctor's office visit gets a CPT code, but the wheelchair, the shot medicine, and the knee brace all get Level II codes.

### Question 23

Ambulance rides are reported with A codes, which is the letter for transportation and supplies.

### Question 24

The medicine given by shot gets a J code on the bill; the doctor's visit gets its own separate CPT code.

### Question 25

G codes are temporary labels used when a new service needs a code before a permanent one is ready.

### Question 26

E0143 starts with E, which is the letter for equipment, so it names the wheelchair the patient is getting.

### Question 27

A J code is the label for a medicine given by shot or IV, so J1100 names an injectable drug.

### Question 28

CPT is the doctor's list, and CMS needed a second list for all the other things patients need, so CMS keeps that second list itself.

### Question 29

K codes are temporary labels for brand-new equipment, like a new kind of wheelchair, before it gets a permanent code.

### Question 30

S and T codes are extra labels that private insurance companies use for things that do not have a regular code yet.

### Question 31

To say an item is for the right side, the office adds the two-letter tag RT to the code.

### Question 32

HCPCS is one big filing system with two drawers: CPT for doctor work, and Level II for supplies, medicines, and equipment.

### Question 33

Feeding formulas that go through a tube are reported with B codes, the letter for special nutrition therapy.

### Question 34

V codes are for eye, ear, and speech services, like glasses, hearing aids, and speech therapy.

### Question 35

Supplies like surgical trays get an A code, the letter for the small items used in patient care.

### Question 36

D codes point to dental work, connecting the medical coding list to the dental coding list.

### Question 37

An artificial limb is reported with an L code, the letter for braces and artificial body parts.

### Question 38

The first letter is like a colored tag that says which list the code comes from and what kind of thing it is.

### Question 39

Oxygen machines are equipment, so they get an E code, the letter for equipment.

### Question 40

If the code on the bill is wrong, the insurance might say no, and the patient could wait longer for a wheelchair or medicine they need.

### Question 41

A knee brace is a support device, so it gets an L code, not a code for surgery or a visit.

### Question 42

Level II modifiers can use letters, so they can say more than the numbers-only CPT modifiers, like telling the payer which side an item is for.

### Question 43

The doctor's visit and the medicine are two different things, so they get two different codes on the same bill.

### Question 44

Medicare uses the Level II list to name and pay for wheelchairs, medicines, and supplies, while still using CPT for doctor visits and surgeries.

### Question 45

A wheelchair is equipment, so it needs the equipment (E) code. Putting it under the doctor-procedure list is a mistake.

### Question 46

CPT's list is about what the doctor does, so a second list was made for everything else patients need, like supplies and equipment.

### Question 47

The code on the bill has to match exactly what really happened and what the doctor ordered, like matching the right label to the right box.

### Question 48

When there is no exact label for an item, the office uses a catch-all code and writes down what the item really is.

### Question 49

The Level II list is refreshed like a new phone book every year, and sometimes more often for special new codes.

### Question 50

A walker is a piece of equipment a patient keeps, so it gets an E code.

### Question 51

P codes are for lab and pathology tests, the letter for the lab work.

### Question 52

R codes are for X-ray and imaging services, the letter for radiology.

### Question 53

To say an item is for the left side, the office adds the two-letter tag LT to the code.

### Question 54

DME is equipment you can use over and over, that helps with a medical problem, is made for home, and is not something a healthy person would usually need.

### Question 55

A syringe is thrown away after one use, so it is a supply; a bed, wheelchair, and CPAP are kept and reused, so they are equipment.

### Question 56

The J code says what kind of medicine it is, and the NDC says exactly which brand and box it came from, like a general label plus a barcode.

### Question 57

Different insurance companies want different details, so the assistant follows the office's instructions about which codes to include.

### Question 58

A temporary code is a placeholder label for something new, used until a permanent label is ready.

### Question 59

A replacement limb is billed with an L code, the letter for artificial body parts and braces.

### Question 60

Double-checking the code before sending the bill is like checking an address before mailing a letter, so it does not come back rejected.

### Question 61

A dressing is a supply, so it gets an A code; the wheelchair, shot, and brace each belong in their own letter group.

### Question 62

A national code list means a wheelchair is called the same thing in every state, like having one shared language for billing.

### Question 63

Ambulance rides are reported with A codes, the letter for transportation services.

### Question 64

A is for supplies and rides, and E is for equipment, like the difference between a bandage and a wheelchair.

### Question 65

If the assistant cannot find the right label, the safest move is to ask someone trained in coding for help instead of guessing.

### Question 66

G codes are temporary labels for services, often used by Medicare, until a permanent code exists.

### Question 67

A Level II code is one letter plus four numbers, like E0143.

### Question 68

Some codes need a small extra tag to be complete, like needing the correct size on a clothing label; the office finds the right tag and re-sends the bill.

### Question 69

The two codes are like a restaurant bill that lists both the meal and the drink separately; they are different items, not duplicates.

### Question 70

The pump is equipment (E), the little supplies are A, and the insulin medicine is J, so each part gets its own label.

### Question 71

A temporary code is a placeholder for something new, used until the permanent label is ready.

### Question 72

When a bed claim is denied, the office usually finds the problem in the code, a missing side tag, or missing paperwork that proves the bed is needed.

### Question 73

If the thing being billed is a supply, medicine, or equipment with no doctor-procedure code, it belongs on the Level II list.

### Question 74

A9270 is a catch-all label for a supply with no exact code, so the office has to write down what the supply really is.

### Question 75

When insurance asks for proof, the office sends the doctor's order and records that show the item was really needed.

### Question 76

RT and LT are like writing right or left on a pair of shoes so the store knows you bought one of each, not two of the same.

### Question 77

If the assistant is not sure which code is right, they ask a coding expert instead of guessing, because a wrong guess can cause real problems.

### Question 78

A CPAP is equipment the patient uses at home every night, so it gets an E code.

### Question 79

Level I is the doctor's list (CPT) and Level II is the supplies-and-equipment list; they are two different drawers.

### Question 80

The nebulizer machine gets an E code and the liquid medicine gets a J code, two separate labels on the bill.

### Question 81

The E is the equipment letter, so E0143 tells the reviewer the code names a piece of equipment.

### Question 82

Level II gives each supply and piece of equipment its own exact label, so the office does not have to use a vague catch-all code.

### Question 83

To tell the payer which foot the insert is for, the office adds RT for right or LT for left to the code.

### Question 84

Putting the wrong item's code on the bill, like labeling a walker as a wheelchair, is the kind of mistake that gets a bill rejected.

### Question 85

HCPCS is the big shared language for naming everything in healthcare, from doctor visits to wheelchairs to medicines, so bills can be sent and paid.
